title: I'm Ambivalent About "The Science of Learning"
author: fivetwelvethirteen
summary: A teacher who grew up stuttering uses his own experience with ineffective versus effective speech therapy to argue that 'the science of learning,' despite genuinely improving his teaching through concepts like cognitive load and retrieval practice, is being oversold relative to how much is actually known. He invokes Benjamin Bloom's argument that a bell-curve distribution of outcomes signals unsuccessful instruction, not a natural law, and argues that most classroom teaching remains 'unsuccessful' in Bloom's sense, with phonics as a rare, well-evidenced exception rather than the rule. Using the parable of blind men describing an elephant, he argues teachers only have secure knowledge of a few 'parts' of the science of learning, while most of what actually determines whether a lesson works is 'one part science and three parts empiricism' -- trial-and-error craft knowledge that hasn't been, and may not be able to be, codified. He closes by refusing to oversell his own enthusiasm: while he'll keep sharing what cognitive science has taught him, he won't tell others that 'the science of learning' alone can fix the profession.
points: Uses his own experience with a stutter and years of ineffective versus one instance of highly effective speech therapy to argue that 'generic strategies' fail where content-specific, often counterintuitive craft knowledge succeeds.

Invokes Benjamin Bloom's claim that a bell-curve distribution of student outcomes reflects 'unsuccessful instruction,' not inevitability, arguing that most classroom teaching reinforces where students started rather than shifting the whole distribution upward.

Uses phonics as the sharpest example of the 'science of learning' elephant parable: it's one part of the elephant researchers genuinely understand well, while most of teaching remains 'one part science and three parts empiricism.'

Explicitly declines to oversell his own enthusiasm for cognitive science research, arguing that telling teachers 'if only more understood the science of learning' overstates how much is actually known well enough to reliably change outcomes.
quotes: On the other side, I worry that the science of learning overpromises. Is there, truly, a science of learning? How much do we know about learning?

This is something I've found with a lot of effective teaching. It's not a generic strategy like break learning into small steps. Effective teaching is rooted in an understanding of the specific content to be taught.

There is nothing sacred about the normal curve. It is the distribution most appropriate to chance and random activity. Education is a purposeful activity and we seek to have the students learn what we have to teach.
I think that what Bloom called unsuccessful instruction is the norm. The bell curve is what most outcomes look like in education.
We know some stuff. We can describe a bit about the general shape of the thing that we might call the science of learning. But most of the specifics are yet to be filled in.
But the nitty-gritty practical knowledge that helps me put that stuff into practice in my classroom is full of lessons learned from trial and error, one part science and three parts empiricism.
